metadata.title: Predicting STEM competencies with machine learning: identifying key determinants among 522,802 adolescents

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available OECD PISA 2022 dataset and analyzes 15-year-old students across 66 economies, after excluding cases with missing values on student-, family-, and school-level variables. The manuscript describes data cleaning, imputation, normalization, and a train/test split (80/20) but does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the ML training or evaluation. Because the models are standard scikit-learn classifiers (e.g., XGBoost, Random Forest) and the paper does not specify weight-aware estimation, it is unclear whether complex survey design effects were incorporated; analysts should consult the PISA 2022 technical documentation for appropriate weight variables (e.g., student weights) when conducting population-representative inference. For replication, the recommended approach is to apply PISA student weights in any weighted evaluation/aggregation step, or explicitly justify an unweighted ML pipeline if weights are omitted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample drawn from PISA 2022 student microdata for 15-year-olds across 66 participating economies. Inclusion followed a flowchart: (1) start with all participants in the PISA 2022 student dataset; (2) exclude students with missing values across student-level variables; (3) exclude students with missing values across family-level variables; (4) exclude students with missing values across school-level variables; after these selections, the final estimation sample comprised 522,802 students. In preprocessing, variables with invalid, skipped, not applicable, or not reached responses were coded as system missing; countries with entire missing responses (0) to any variables at student-, family-, and school-levels were dropped. The dataset was then loaded into Python for cleaning, imputation, and normalization prior to model training.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) STEM competencies (average of mathematics and science achievement)
main_findings.target_variable: STEM competencies (high vs low; global-mean threshold)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: XGBoost — Accuracy: 0.783, Precision: 0.771, Recall: 0.784, F1: 0.777; AUC: 0.85. Other models (test set): Naive Bayes Accuracy 0.694 (F1 0.712), Decision Tree Accuracy 0.719 (F1 0.718), Logistic Regression Accuracy 0.733 (F1 0.727), AdaBoost Accuracy 0.769 (F1 0.759), Random Forest Accuracy 0.764 (F1 0.755).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged home possessions, student employment, gender, cognitive activation for reasoning, and mathematics anxiety to predict STEM competencies (high vs low), finding that XGBoost achieved the highest test performance (Accuracy 78.3%, F1 77.7%, AUC 0.85). This indicates that strengthening home learning resources, reducing time/constraints from part-time work, and addressing mathematics anxiety—while also promoting cognitive-activation instructional practices—may improve students’ STEM competency profiles, though the cross-sectional design and SHAP-based importance do not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students across 66 economies (final analytic sample: 522,802) and constructs STEM competencies by averaging mathematics (AVGMATH) and science (AVGSCIE) achievement, then dichotomizing into high vs low using the global mean threshold. Six supervised ML classifiers (Naïve Bayes, Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) were trained on an 80/20 train/test split with hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV and feature selection using XGBoost-based elimination and RFECV, evaluated with Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, and AUC. XGBoost outperformed all alternatives, reaching Accuracy 78.3%, F1 77.7%, and AUC 0.85. The most influential predictors (via SHAP) included home possessions, student employment, gender, cognitive activation for reasoning, and mathematics anxiety, with SHAP interaction suggesting a slight moderation by gender for anxiety effects. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature (no causal inference) and unclear incorporation of PISA complex survey weights in the ML pipeline.
